_what: Precision measurements of looks-clean on foreign projects. Every verdict was reached by reading the code at the cited line. This file is data, not a test: test/readme.mjs checks that the README quotes it correctly and that each measurement adds up.
_method: Projects are picked BEFORE the tool is run, on one stated criterion, and none of them is the author’s own.

THE CRITERION IS DENSITY OF EXTERNAL READS, not density of error handling. Rules 2 and 3 group handlers and reads by the family of external operation, so a codebase full of try/catch around its own arithmetic gives them nothing to compare. Measured: fastify has 113 error handlers and 8 external reads, and reported nothing at all. Count the reads first.
Shallow clone, default settings, no config file, no exclusions beyond the built-in list.
The FIRST TEN findings of each run, in the order the tool printed them, are read in the source and judged.
Ten checked out of N reported is ten checked. It is not the precision of the tool over the whole run, and nothing here claims that it is.
A project that reports nothing is a result and is recorded with the reason. A zero for a reason that is not about precision — the wrong shape of project, or a defect in the tool — says so.
_twoNumbers: Two measurements from two runs are kept side by side rather than one number corrected. The tool changed between them — test directories are now excluded by default — and so did the material. A single revised figure would hide both facts.

measurements.toolState: before test directories were excluded by default (13 built-in exclusions)

projects.name: got
projects.whyChosen: Rule 3 needs a population of reads that MIXES guarded and unguarded. An HTTP client is where deadlines live, so if the rule works anywhere it should work here.
projects.note: 350 of the 359 findings are under test/. All ten checked were test code.

projects.name: uptime-kuma
projects.whyChosen: An application rather than a library: network and database reads in the same files, ninety-odd notification providers written to one shape, which is the densest population of comparable error handlers I could find.

projects.name: eslint
projects.whyChosen: File-system heavy, and it is the tool this project defines itself against. If looks-clean produces nonsense on eslint's own source, that is worth knowing and worth printing.

findings.why: A priming request inside a cache test. The test file is treated as a layer, but a test file's shape is dictated by what each test is testing.
got('prime') warms a keep-alive agent before the timeout under test. A deadline here would break the test.
The test asserts that a slow upload does not trip the response timeout. Having no request deadline is the subject of the test.
Priming request again, same shape as rank 2.
Priming request again.
http.request inside a request hook whose enclosing got() call carries timeout: {request: 100}. The deadline is on the caller and the rule reads the statement.
An HTTP/2 negotiation test. No deadline is intended.
Same shape as rank 6: the enclosing call sets timeout: {request: timeout}.
Same shape as rank 6.
http.request inside a retry hook; the enclosing call governs the deadline.

The reported 'answer' is `retries = 0`, a loop counter reset inside a long monitor-beat catch. No caller ever receives it, and the family was attributed from some read elsewhere in the same try block.

`} catch (e) {}` around the TLS certificate comparison. A failure there is discarded whole, and the result is a certificate change that looks like no change. Eleven of the twelve handlers in the file do better. eslint no-empty would also find it.
`catch (e) { webhookHasAvatar = true; }` with a comment saying why. The failure is absorbed on purpose and the consequence is an avatar. The tool has no notion of what the value is used for.
A copy of rank 3 in a second provider. Duplicated code produces duplicated findings.

`try { connection.end(); } catch (_) { connection.destroy(); }`. The handler acts on the failure — it escalates the close — but acting is not on the tool's list of traces, which is logging, rethrowing, using the binding, or a tagged answer.
The same cleanup in a second function of the same file.

`execFile(..., { timeout })` — the deadline is there, written as an ES6 shorthand property. The deadline table looks for `timeout:` with a colon and misses `{ timeout }`. A defect in the tool, not in the code.

Malformed custom headers become `{}`, which is also what no headers looks like. The monitor then runs with the wrong request and reports UP. The two neighbouring JSON.parse handlers in the same directory rethrow.
The handler sends `response.status(400).json(...)` and then returns bare. Rule 2 reads the return value and sees `undefined`; the caller here is an HTTP client that was told exactly what happened.
An empty catch with a comment saying the blobs are handled elsewhere. peers=0/0 — no neighbour comparison was made, so this is rule 1 at its weakest, which the ranking floors but does not suppress.

printResults returns false on three failure paths and true on success; there is no 'found nothing' path at all. The tool counted `if (await isDirectory(filePath)) { ...; return false; }` as the empty path, because a failure detected by a plain predicate is not a catch and not an error-named branch.
A documented fallback: if the message template will not load, the code below uses error.stack instead. peers=0/0.
An optional-dependency probe guarded by an isAvailable flag. The record of the failure is the flag NOT being set, which the tool cannot see.

`fsp.stat(filePath).catch(...)` is reported once as `fsp.stat.catch` and once as `fsp.stat`. The fs family matches on the receiver prefix, so every method chained onto an fs call counts as a further read — inflating the population and printing the same line twice.
The second half of rank 4: the same line, the same read.
`fs.lstatSync` is synchronous and cannot take a deadline in any spelling, so it can only ever be counted as deviating. The fs family does not separate sync from async.
`try { structuredClone(options); return; } catch { /* continue */ }` — the failure is the signal to fall through to the code that finds WHICH key is uncloneable and throws a better error.
A deliberate 'ignore syntax errors in RegExp' in a lint rule whose job is to survive unparseable patterns.
A test FIXTURE: a file whose entire purpose is to be an odd shape for the parser to chew on. Reporting it is reporting the test data.
Another parser fixture, same as rank 9.

test-layer.note: Test files and test fixtures compared as if one engineering decision governed them.

deadline-one-frame-out.note: The deadline is set on the enclosing call and the read sits in a callback that call was handed.

rule-1-with-no-population.note: Rule 1 speaks without neighbours by design. Every one of these is a documented deliberate decision.

compensating-action.note: The handler acts on the failure instead of reporting it; acting is not on the list of traces.

deliberate-cosmetic-default.note: The tool has no notion of what the defaulted value is used for.

tool-bug-chained-read-counted-twice.note: The fs family prefix-matches the receiver.

tool-bug-shorthand-timeout.note: `{ timeout }` shorthand is not recognised as a deadline.

tool-bug-sync-call-cannot-be-guarded.note: A *Sync read can never carry a deadline and should never be a deviation.

answer-is-bookkeeping.note: A local counter assignment in a long handler was read as the handler's answer.

answer-through-a-side-channel.note: The handler answered with an HTTP 400; rule 2 reads only the return value.

predicate-failure-read-as-empty.note: A failure detected by a plain predicate is filed as the empty path.

excludingTestsWouldRemove.note: All ten of got's checked findings and both of eslint's fixture findings are test code; 350 of got's 359 findings in total are under test/. Test code is not in the built-in exclusions today.

measurements.commonFactor: In twenty of the twenty-eight false alarms the failure IS handled — a deadline on the enclosing call, an HTTP 400, a compensating destroy(), a documented fallback, or a test whose whole subject is the missing deadline. The tool judges a handler by the shape of its own body and by the value it returns, and neither of those shows where the failure actually went.

measurements.toolState: after test directories were excluded by default (19 built-in exclusions)
measurements.whyDifferent: Two things changed at once and the README says so: test code is no longer read, and the material is three different projects. The first change removed the largest single source of noise in the earlier measurement; the second means these are not two readings of the same thing.
measurements.weakerThanTheFirst: Ten findings checked, not thirty, because two of the three projects reported nothing at all — and neither zero was about precision. A thinner measurement is reported as a thinner measurement.
measurements.criterionRefined: Density of error handling was not a sharp enough criterion. Rules 2 and 3 need handlers OVER EXTERNAL READS. fastify has 113 error handlers and 8 external reads, because a web framework receives calls rather than making them, and it produced nothing. The next measurement should select on reads, not on handlers.

projects.name: node-red
projects.whyChosen: A platform that loads and runs third-party nodes: file system, child processes and HTTP in one codebase.
projects.zeroBecause: The tool read 11 files of a repository holding 308 JavaScript source files, and said nothing about it. node-red keeps its source under packages/node_modules/, and the built-in **/node_modules/** exclusion swallowed all of it. This is a defect in the tool of exactly the class it reports: it printed "findings: 0" where it meant "I did not look". Recorded and left unfixed.

projects.name: verdaccio
projects.whyChosen: A server with a storage layer: file system, network and auth in one repository, and a plugin architecture that repeats the same shapes, which is what a population needs.

projects.name: fastify
projects.whyChosen: Dense error handling by reputation, and a different character again: a framework rather than an application or a server.
projects.zeroBecause: A legitimate zero, and the most useful thing in this measurement. 113 error handlers and 8 external reads: a web framework RECEIVES calls rather than making them, so rules 2 and 3 have almost nothing to group. The run said so — four sites passed over, four layers with no convention — rather than printing a bare zero.

findings.why: fs.mkdirSync("/") on an in-memory filesystem, with "ignore if already exists". The failure is the expected outcome of an idempotent setup step.

folderExists() answers false when the stat throws, so a permission error and an absent directory become the same answer and the caller goes on to try creating it. Mild — a reviewer could close it as the contract of a predicate — but the claim is accurate and the debug() line does not reach the caller.
fileExists(), the same shape as rank 2 in the same file. Two findings, one piece of copy-paste.
fs.createWriteStream is a WRITE and a stream constructor, not a read, and no deadline belongs on it. The fs family matches on the receiver, so every fs.* call counts as a read.
fs.fstatSync is synchronous and cannot carry a deadline in any spelling. The comment two lines above explains why it is synchronous on purpose.

A failed JWT verification leaves credentials undefined, and the _isRemoteUserValid(credentials) check four lines down is the record. The most arguable of the ten: the maintainers own FIXME comment sits on the line the tool picked.
A console.warn naming the missing language file sits four lines below the handler, outside it. The tool reads the handler body only.
The fall-through IS the handling, and the default return two lines below is the record.
The comment says the stream error event surfaces any real problem. The failure is reported through an event channel the tool cannot follow.
A JSON parse failure is the signal to try the legacy user:password format. The failure is not lost, it is the branch condition.

record-is-elsewhere-in-the-function.note: The record of the failure sits outside the handler body — a console.warn below it, an undefined check, a stream error event. The tool reads the handler and the value it returns.

fs-family-matches-any-fs-call.note: Every fs.* call is treated as a read, including writes, stream constructors and *Sync calls that can never carry a deadline. The same root cause as two of the first measurement tool defects.

failure-is-the-expected-outcome.note: An idempotent setup step whose failure means the work was already done.

failure-is-the-control-flow.note: The failure is the branch condition, not an error.

measurements.commonFactor: Five of the eight false alarms record the failure somewhere the tool does not read: a console.warn four lines below the handler, an undefined check, a stream error event, or the fall-through itself. That is the first measurement common factor sharpened — the tool reads the handler body and its return value, and in real code the record of a failure is very often just outside both.

fixedAfterwards.defect: a project whose source sits under an excluded directory gets a silent zero
fixedAfterwards.how: Every run that excluded anything now reports how many source files sat behind the exclusions, names the three largest with the pattern that removed them, and adds a louder sentence when more source was excluded than read. On node-red the run now says: 741 files behind 12 excluded directories, largest packages/node_modules/@node-red/ (>=500, **/node_modules/**).
fixedAfterwards.whyThisOneAndNotTheOthers: The other four defects change WHICH findings come out, so fixing them and re-measuring on the same material would be tuning to the test. This one changes no finding at all — it adds a sentence about what was not read — and it is the tool committing its own subject, which cannot be left standing to protect a number.
fixedAfterwards.guardedBy: test/resilience.mjs, scenario "sources under an excluded directory". Removing the fix turns that scenario SILENT, which fails the layer.

_changeChecks: A change to the tool that could move a number is measured on the SAME material before and after, and the result is kept whichever way it came out. A measurement is only worth the runs nobody was allowed to discard.

changeChecks.change: The peer ladder now climbs a rung when the group it found has no convention, not only when the group is too small to speak.
changeChecks.why: Two silences were treated as one kind. A group below minpop was retried one rung out; a group big enough whose members all did the same thing was not, and the site was passed over. Both are the same sentence — this layer cannot answer the question.
changeChecks.method: Both recorded measurements' material, all six projects at the revisions they name. Default settings, no config file. The tool was run at the commit before this change and at the commit after it, and the two runs were compared finding by finding.
changeChecks.verdict: Not one JavaScript finding changed, so precision on this material cannot have changed. Nothing was re-judged because there was nothing new to judge.
changeChecks.whyNothingChanged: The change only bites where a file agrees with itself and its directory does not. Across all six projects that happened 0 times. Where a JavaScript project sets no deadlines it sets none anywhere, so the silence is a property of the project rather than of the file, and the rung above is as silent as the rung below. The Java case that motivated the change is the opposite shape: FileManager.java collapses every one of its four file-system handlers, while 3 of the 23 in its directory carry their outcome.
changeChecks.coverage: The finding-by-finding comparison covers all four rules. The climb-opportunity count below covers three of them: swallowed, default-on-error and no-timeout. same-answer is left out of that breakdown because its groups are built from state the rule computes internally, and the comparison above already covers it.
changeChecks.notMeasured: This says nothing about precision in Java, where the change does move findings. That is measured separately before 0.2.0 ships.

changeChecks.change: A read wrapped in a nested try is no longer attributed to the handler outside it. The outer catch never sees that failure, and because the nested call is also the last read in source order it was winning the label every time.
changeChecks.why: The report named the wrong call. FileManager.getFilesFromFolder opens Files.newDirectoryStream and, inside the stream, calls Files.readAttributes in a try of its own; the finding told the reader to go and look at readAttributes, whose IOException it never sees. A finding whose sentence is false is not a weaker finding, it is a wrong one.
changeChecks.method: Both recorded measurements' material, all six projects at the revisions they name, default settings, before and after. Compared finding by finding INCLUDING the label and the family, because the label is what this change is about. The recorded golden runs were re-run unchanged.
changeChecks.verdict: No JavaScript finding changed, label included, and the four golden runs matched field by field.
changeChecks.belowTheFindings: Findings are the tip, so the attribution itself was counted underneath them. Of 215 JavaScript handlers standing over a read, 1 changed: uptime-kuma extra/release/generate-changelog.mjs:251, which lost its family because both JSON.parse calls in its try sit in a nested try of their own (lines 226-236). Read at the cited lines, the new answer is the right one. In Java 7 of 45 changed, one of them to no family at all: a handler whose body wraps every file probe in a catch of its own, so the outer one was being credited with reads it cannot see. Read at the line, the new answer is the right one; the location is withheld for the reason languageSamples gives.
changeChecks.notMeasured: Whether the seven Java attributions that moved are each right was checked by reading two of them, not all seven. The Java precision sample taken before 0.2.0 reads findings, and these sit underneath findings.

changeChecks.change: Rule 4 no longer treats a guard on an argument as the empty path, and no longer speaks about a function that has no answer to give.
changeChecks.why: Both were measured, not suspected. Every false alarm in the Java sample came from rule 4 and from these two shapes: five of the six in the first twenty were a parameter guard colliding with a catch, and two were a void method whose returns are identical by construction.
changeChecks.method: Both recorded measurements' JavaScript material at the revisions they name, before and after, compared finding by finding including label. Java measured on two corpora: the 21 files the false alarms were found in, and the other 96 files of the same tree, which no verdict in this file was ever read from.
changeChecks.verdict: No JavaScript finding changed. Rule 4 fires once in the six projects and the correction does not touch it.
changeChecks.oneNumberMoved: uptime-kuma counted 619 sites passed over before and 613 after. Six functions whose only normal exit was a guard leave rule 4's contest altogether, so they are no longer counted as passed over. No finding moved with them.

rule4ByCorpus.corpus: java, the 21 files the false alarms came from
java, the other 96 files of the same tree

changeChecks.aimedRatherThanQuietened: The correction was checked against the verdicts already recorded in languageSamples, one by one. Of the SIX rule-4 findings judged real, none was removed. Of the SEVEN judged noise, six were removed. The seventh (J-14) keeps its finding and re-anchors onto a real empty path further down the same method — the slot it genuinely failed to find — so it stops being a false alarm rather than disappearing. A correction that removed a real finding, or that removed the seventh by silencing it, would have shown up here.
changeChecks.whatThisDoesNotShow: That precision improved. Six false alarms out of fourteen left the Java corpus, and the eight that remain have not been read again. The sample in languageSamples was taken against the tool as it stood on 2026-09-21 and is kept at that date rather than adjusted; a number for 0.2.1 needs a fresh sample, judged the same way, which has not been taken.
changeChecks.negativeFixture: test/fixtures/clean/Preconditions.java holds all three shapes beside three neighbours that make the silence mean something: it reports three findings without the correction and none with it. A negative fixture that is quiet because nothing in it was comparable proves nothing, so the peer group reaches minpop and a convention exists.

_languageSamples: A precision sample taken when a new language is added, before the version that claims to support it ships. Three verdicts, not two: a site can be a defect, a deliberate and defensible choice, or a finding the tool should not have made. Only the last is noise.

languageSamples.material: VideoAnalyzer before its commit 6bf5971 — 21 files of one directory, not the author's own code but the author's own product
languageSamples.run: scan <that directory> --config test/fixtures/golden.config.json, default layer and minpop, no other flags
languageSamples.method: TWO SAMPLES OF TWENTY, KEPT APART. The first is drawn at random, because a reader runs the tool and reads the whole list, not its top; the second is the first twenty in the printed order, which is how the JavaScript measurements were taken, so the two methods can be compared rather than averaged.
languageSamples.selection: FNV-1a(seed) seeds an xorshift32; a Fisher-Yates over the printed order; take the first twenty. The printed order is itself deterministic (score, then file, line, rule, anchor), so the seed and the snapshot reproduce the same twenty.

verdicts.real: a caller or the user can be shown a wrong state because of this site
verdicts.deliberate: the collapse is real and the author chose it, with a comment or a pattern applied uniformly, and the consequence is confined
verdicts.noise: the tool should not have made this finding — its claim about the site is false or vacuous

languageSamples.threshold: Agreed before the sample was drawn: if noise in the RANDOM sample exceeds half, 0.2.0 does not ship until the vocabulary is corrected.
languageSamples.result: Noise 3 of 20 in the random sample, 6 of 20 in the first twenty. Below the threshold either way.
languageSamples.whereTheNoiseIs: All of it is in rule 4 (same-answer), in both samples. Rules 1, 2 and 3 produced no noise at all in 36 distinct findings read. Not one false alarm was traced to a dictionary entry — no wrong family, no wrong ambiguous value — so the correction is to the rule, not to the vocabulary the last two commits built.
languageSamples.theTopIsWorseThanTheMiddle: The first twenty holds MORE noise than the random twenty, not less, which is the opposite of what a top-of-the-list sample is usually accused of. Rule 4 scores highest and rule 4 is where all the noise is, so the ranking puts the least reliable rule on the first screen — the placement scan.mjs already warns about for a different rule.
twoCorrectionsImplied: A parameter or precondition guard is not the empty path. `if (x == null) return null` answers a caller who asked a malformed question; colliding it with a catch that answers null produces a finding about nothing. Five of the six false alarms in the first sample are this.
A void function has no answer, so its two paths cannot differ. Rule 4 has nothing to say about one and should not speak.
languageSamples.notMeasured: Whether the 53 findings outside both samples hold up. Twenty checked at random out of eighty-nine is twenty checked.
languageSamples.locations:
THE VERDICTS ARE PUBLISHED, THE LOCATIONS ARE NOT. Fourteen of the twenty in the random sample are real defects in a product that is sold, and most of them are still unfixed; a file and a line beside each would be a public bug list for somebody else's customers to read. So every site carries a stable identifier J-01..J-34 instead. What a finding was judged, by which rule, and why a false alarm was false is all here and unchanged — the sample can be argued with. Only where it points is withheld.
The identifiers are assigned in alphabetical order of the location, so the numbering carries neither the verdict nor the rank, and consecutive ones may share a file. The map from identifier to file and line lives with the product, outside this repository, at docs/looks-clean-sample-map.json in the checkout that answer 7 already names — so anybody holding that checkout can still check every row against the code.
